articles.title: A robot called GIMLI will explore a lunar cave for a future moon base
articles.summary: The race to build a moon base is ramping up. Columnist Robin George Andrews explores how NASA is preparing by sending a cave-hunting robot ahead of humans
articles.content:
Artist’s illustration of NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter peering down into a lava tube Elaboration of a photo of A. Romeo. LRO 3D model by NASA (Brian Kumanchik, Christian Lopez. NASA/JPL-Caltech), Earthrise photo captured on Taken on 24 December 1968, 16:40 UTC by Apollo 8 astronaut Bill Anders

In video-game terms, the moon is the first level in an unfathomably giant, never-ending realm. It is the place where we, the players, learn the controls and try very hard not to die, in preparation for safely exploring the rest of the solar system. At a convenient 385,000 kilometres from Earth – a stone’s throw in cosmic terms – our planet’s companion is a great testing ground. And the race is on to claim a piece of it for a base.

Unfortunately for us, the moon is also a preposterously dangerous place to be. The volcanic dust there is adhesive, abrasive and corrosive, able to eat through spacesuits and machinery like a swarm of voracious locusts. Its daytime temperature can reach 120°C, while its benighted craters can plunge to -245°C, which is close to absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature in the universe. There are moonquakes, which (unlike Earth’s own tremors) can last for tens of minutes. And its lack of an atmosphere means that its surface is unprotected from asteroids (which can splatter you) and space radiation (which can give you cancer).

There are so many awful ways to perish on the moon. China knows the risks. So does the US. And yet, these two countries – along with their many friends and enemies – aren’t just keen on sending astronauts to the lunar surface; they are also planning to establish their own nuclear-powered bases, home to rotating astronaut crews.

Advertisement

I know what you’re thinking: this sounds like the stuff of science fiction, in the sense that you think it will never happen or, if you do, you suspect that it will go horribly, dramatically wrong. But I have been covering these plans for several years now, and I can promise you two things. The first is that, because this new space race is being (partly, perhaps largely) driven by nationalistic zeal, a moon base is much closer to being realised than you might think. The second is that you’re right: if space agencies aren’t exceedingly careful, things could go wrong.

Neither side wants to see a dead astronaut on the lunar surface, which is why these bases must be nothing short of impregnable fortresses. To that end, NASA recently announced that it has selected three new uncrewed scientific missions to the moon, each designed to further the goals of its Artemis programme. The first is a sophisticated seismometer, which will listen out for moonquakes and meteorite impacts. The second will hunt for signs of ice that can be turned into potable water, breathable oxygen and rocket fuel.

So far, so expected. But the third robotic mission really stood out to me, because it is going to investigate a subterranean lava tube.

Yes, you read that right: a tube, burrowed out by actual lava, on the moon.

Lava tubes are extremely cool – and I’m not just saying that because I’m a trained volcanologist. I have walked through several on Earth. They’re serpentine, cavernous things. They often form when a scorching-hot river of molten rock is rushing through a channel. When the river runs out of momentum or magma, the top – exposed to the atmosphere – cools quickly, forming a roof. The rest of the lava drains out elsewhere, leaving an eerie, inky-black hollow behind. Some of them even have nice acoustics, which makes them great alternative gig venues.

The moon is a great big ball of frozen magma. It’s geologically comatose today, but a stegosaurus could have looked up and seen the crimson glow of freshly erupted lava painting the lunar surface. And where there’s an abundance of lava, there are oodles of lava tubes. The problem is that, from the perspective of NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter satellite, suspected lava tube sites just look like deep, shadowy pits.

The Marius Hills pit, on the moon’s nearside, is a prime example. It looks like someone punched a hole in the lunar surface, which is why it’s thought to be a natural skylight for a lava tube. Keen to find out for sure, NASA is sending a robotic mission there to scout it out – and not just to settle a few bets between lunar geologists.

NASA notes that lava tubes offer “natural, ready-made shelters that provide crucial thermal stability and shielding from deadly ionizing radiation and micrometeoroid bombardment”. That’s right: one day, NASA’s astronauts might be living in ancient volcanic vaults to avoid spending too much time on its truly terrible surface.

The mission to the Marius Hills pit – the first plan to explore a lunar lava tube – doesn’t have a launch date just yet. But it does have an excellent name: the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation, or GIMLI. Yes, that one, the warrior dwarf from Middle-earth who loves his axe, despises evil rings of power and frequents all kinds of dangerous caves.

I reached out to Nathaniel Putzig at the Planetary Science Institute, the principal investigator of GIMLI. He swears that the name wasn’t inspired by J. R. R. Tolkien’s Lord of the Rings. He says that he simply wrote down words describing the mission plan and arranged them to make a pleasing sounding acronym.

“At the time, I was only vaguely aware of the Tolkien association, not fully realising that I had happened upon the name for legendary dwarf Gimli, member of the Fellowship of the Ring and the first Lord of the Glittering Caves,” he told me. The name, he said, “won out in the ranked choice voting by team members”. Thank goodness, because it’s literally perfect for this mission.

GIMLI is a joint effort between the Planetary Science Institute, NASA, the Norwegian Space Agency and US tech firm Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. It won’t abseil into the pit itself. Instead, it will land next to it and use its suite of instruments – including a ground-penetrating radar, seismic sensors and a device that measures subtle differences in the moon’s gravitational field – to map out the hidden subsurface, while its cameras take shots of the pit and its walls.

Presuming the skylight does lead to a lava tube, GIMLI won’t just scratch a scientific itch. It will inform NASA’s plans to keep its astronauts from being murdered by the moon.

The Marius Hills pit looks like a bullet hole in the moon’s surface Credit: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University

Car-sized asteroids burn up in Earth’s atmosphere without consequence. But on the moon, they slam, unimpeded, into the ground, and explode like a pile of dynamite. Very rarely – as happened in 2024 – an asteroid the size of a couple of football stadiums crashes into the lunar surface with the force of an atomic bomb. Astronauts are far more likely to be imperilled by pebble-sized asteroids, which sound like less of an issue until you realise that they travel at tens of thousands of kilometres per hour, effectively making them hypersonic space bullets. Fortunately, the roof of a lava tube would handily absorb their impacts.

If the ceiling of frozen lava was thick enough, it would also offer protection from a major solar storm. When the sun is feeling irritable, it can launch a salvo of super-charged particles our way. Earth’s magnetic field and substantial atmosphere deflect and soak up many of them. But the exposed moon takes these bombardments head on. In the event of an especially intense solar outburst, astronauts there could receive a fatal dose and die weeks or even days later of acute radiation sickness. Hiding in a lava tube could save their lives.

Thank goodness, then, that the GIMLI project exists, and can help us answer the many questions we still have. What are the moon’s lava tubes like? Are they roomy? Do they look stable? Could you fit an astronaut habitat in them, or a small nuclear reactor that powers a nearby base? Seeking these havens out is, in NASA’s words, “important groundwork for safe, long‑term living on the moon”.

NASA is targeting the lunar south pole for its upcoming crewed Artemis missions. This is where it wants to establish the first moon base, largely because it is thought to be home to crucial reservoirs of water. Should we expect that base to be at least partly concealed in a lava tube?

A 3D model of a lunar cave tunnel, which stretches beneath an open pit

“Lava tubes necessarily form in volcanic terrain, and there is little or no evidence of such terrains in the heavily cratered highlands of the south polar region,” says Putzig. So, probably not. But, he adds, “other outposts may well be established elsewhere that lava tubes may be identified”.

Most lava tubes will also require something like rappels, or makeshift elevators, for astronauts to access them. This creates its own hazard: if a clumsy moonwalker trips, falls and gets stuck in a lava tube, or the machinery malfunctions, there’s a chance that they could die down there. Considering all the other ways the moon could take them out, this would be a pretty embarrassing end.

Lava tubes may be a bit of a hard sell: they could be onerous to find, troublesome to access and potentially a bit bleak to live in. I’m willing to bet that, if you’re going to camp on the moon for several months at a time, you would probably prefer to eschew a dark, volcanic labyrinth for a spot on the surface. Even if you’re at risk of being blasted by tiny space rocks, you at least get to see Earth, and the stars cresting the lunar horizon. Even on the moon, the call of the night sky may prove too bewitching a prospect to pass up.

articles.personality_title: NASA’s robot GIMLI will explore lunar caves to help build safer moon bases
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA and other space agencies are racing to build bases on the moon. The moon is very dangerous with extreme temperatures, sharp dust, and radiation, making it hard for astronauts to live there safely.

**What happened** – NASA has chosen a new robot mission called GIMLI (Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation) to explore a deep hole on the moon’s surface. This hole is believed to be an entrance to a lava tube, a natural cave formed by ancient flowing lava. GIMLI will land near the hole and use special tools like radar and cameras to map the inside without going in.

**Impact** – Lava tubes could be perfect shelters for astronauts because they protect from extreme heat, cold, radiation, and space rocks hitting the moon’s surface. Exploring these caves will help NASA decide if they can safely build moon bases inside them. This is an important step toward living on the moon for longer times.

**What’s next step** – GIMLI’s findings will guide future missions and plans for moon bases. If lava tubes are safe and roomy, NASA might build habitats or power stations inside them. Meanwhile, NASA continues other missions to study moon ice and moonquakes to prepare for human visits.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s GIMLI robot will explore lunar caves that could become protective homes for future astronauts on the moon.

articles.title: Evidence of active volcanoes on Mars may boost chances of finding life
articles.summary: Recent fractures on the surface of Mars and gases detected by an orbiter probe provide some of the strongest evidence yet that the planet is volcanically active
articles.content:
Recent fractures on the surface of Mars and gases detected by an orbiter probe provide some of the strongest evidence yet that the planet is volcanically active

Evidence of volcanic activity was detected near Alba Mons on Mars Mars Express & HRSC

Mars may be volcanically active, say scientists who have linked evidence of gases often produced by magma with photographs of fresh fissures found on the surface of the Red Planet. The findings could be interpreted as good news in the hunt for life, as a continuous heat source would be needed to keep microorganisms safe from frigid temperatures on the surface.

Scientists have seen evidence of volcanoes on Mars in the past few million years and seismic activity has hinted that some may still be active, but no evidence of lava flows or current eruptions had previously been found.

In 2019, the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter detected evidence of hydrogen chloride (HCl) in Mars’s atmosphere. That gas is commonly associated with magmatic vents on Earth, and researchers wondered if the same was true on Mars.

Advertisement

To investigate further, Daniel Mège at the Polish Academy of Sciences and his colleagues looked at the little data available – just 15 recorded instances of the gas – alongside newly taken photographs of the surface. They were able to link recent, narrow fissures in the Alba Mons region of Mars to the HCl emissions, providing strong evidence of underground lava flow.

To assess whether the HCl could have come from the fissures, the team modelled the wind direction at the time the measurements were taken.

Free newsletter Sign up to Launchpad Sign up to newsletter

“We have 2 kilometres of wind between them, and in this season there are a lot of dust devils. So, the atmosphere is turbulent. It’s an enormous mess,” says Mège.

Nicolas Thomas at the University of Bern, Switzerland, another team member, stresses that until the area is investigated up-close, there will always be doubt about the source of the gas. But, he argues, this finding makes the case for further surface exploration of Mars.

“Suspicion is one thing, proof is better, right?” says Thomas. “I’m a terrible sceptic. Until you put something down there and you actually sniff the stuff coming out of the ground, you haven’t got unambiguous proof.”

Thomas thinks the finding makes the prospects for life on Mars more likely. “We know that Mars, even at the equator, can be −70°C, −80°C at night. It’s a very harsh environment,” he says. “If this thermal source were constant and continuous, then you have to admit it’s improving the situation [in terms of the hunt for life].”

“This is definitely a highly interesting finding,” says Lena Noack at the Free University of Berlin. “Many scientists working on Mars will not be too surprised, as the picture of a ‘dead’ Mars was inconsistent with many recent research findings.”

This finding has broad implications for the search for extraterrestrial life and future Mars exploration, offering hopeful and inspiring prospects for humanity's understanding of life beyond Earth.
articles.personality_title: New signs of active volcanoes on Mars raise hopes for life
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long studied Mars to understand if it could support life. One key factor is whether the planet still has active volcanoes, which can provide heat and gases needed by living things.

**What happened** – In 2019, a spacecraft called the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrogen chloride gas in Mars’s atmosphere. This gas is often found near volcanic activity on Earth. Researchers then looked at new photos of the Alba Mons region on Mars and found fresh cracks in the surface. By studying wind patterns, they linked these cracks to the gas, showing evidence of underground lava flows.

**Impact** – This is strong proof that Mars might still have active volcanoes. Since volcanoes produce heat, they could create warm spots where tiny life forms might survive despite Mars’s cold temperatures. This discovery changes our idea of Mars from a dead planet to one that may still be geologically alive.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to send missions closer to these cracks to directly study the gases and ground. Getting samples from the surface could confirm if volcanoes are still active and if conditions could support life.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New discoveries of volcanic gases and fresh surface cracks on Mars suggest it may still be volcanically active, improving chances of finding life there.

articles.title: Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky
articles.summary: November's night sky is packed with celestial wonders, from bright meteor fireballs and a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter to a spectacular supermoon. Meanwhile, NASA's Voyager 1 is making history by becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
articles.content:
November 2026 is packed with celestial events worth watching, from brilliant meteors streaking across the sky to a striking encounter between Mars and Jupiter. NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is also approaching an extraordinary milestone, while a dazzling supermoon will close out the month.

Three meteor showers offer multiple opportunities to catch shooting stars, including occasional fireballs bright enough to stand out dramatically against the night sky. Meanwhile, two of the solar system's most recognizable planets will appear unusually close together just before sunrise.

As if that weren't enough, humanity's most distant spacecraft is reaching a point where radio signals from Earth take an entire day to arrive.

Here's what NASA recommends watching for in November.

November 2026 Skywatching Highlights

Around November 5: The Southern Taurid meteor shower reaches its peak, with the possibility of exceptionally bright fireballs.

Around November 12: The Northern Taurids peak, producing approximately five meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions.

November 15 and 16: Mars and Jupiter appear just 1.2 degrees apart in the southeastern sky before sunrise.

November 17: NASA celebrates Voyager 1's historic distance milestone with its Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day activation.

November 17 and 18: The Leonid meteor shower offers its best viewing opportunities before dawn, after the Moon sets, with potentially 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions.

November 24: A full supermoon illuminates the evening sky, beginning a sequence of three consecutive supermoons.

Three Meteor Showers Could Light Up November's Sky

November gives skywatchers several chances to see meteors flash across the darkness. The first opportunities come from the Southern and Northern Taurids, two related meteor showers that reach their highest activity levels about a week apart.

The Southern Taurids peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12. Both showers get their names from the constellation Taurus, where their meteors appear to originate when viewed from Earth.

Neither shower is especially prolific. Even under excellent conditions, each typically produces only about five meteors per hour. However, the Taurids are known for occasionally producing impressive fireballs, exceptionally bright meteors that can make even a relatively quiet night of skywatching memorable.

The Leonids provide another opportunity later in the month. Their best viewing periods are expected during the early morning hours of November 17 and 18, particularly after the Moon has disappeared below the horizon. Under ideal conditions, observers could see approximately 15 meteors per hour, although actual counts will generally be lower.

For the best chance of spotting meteors, travel somewhere away from bright city lights. Allow your eyes roughly 30 minutes to become accustomed to the darkness, then watch a broad section of the sky rather than concentrating on one small area.

Mars and Jupiter Appear Almost Side by Side

Meteor showers aren't the only reason to get outside before dawn. On November 15 and 16, Mars and Jupiter will create an eye-catching pairing in the southeastern sky.

The two planets will appear separated by only about 1.2 degrees, slightly more than the apparent width of two full Moons placed next to each other.

Jupiter will be the brighter of the two, making it relatively easy to identify. Nearby, Mars will stand out with its characteristic reddish appearance.

No telescope or binoculars will be necessary to enjoy the sight. Both planets should be readily visible to the unaided eye under suitable viewing conditions.

Although they will appear remarkably close from Earth's perspective, Mars and Jupiter remain separated by enormous distances in space. Their apparent proximity is simply a result of their positions along our line of sight.

Watching the planets over several consecutive mornings will reveal another interesting feature of their motion. They will gradually appear to move closer together before their positions shift and they begin separating again.

Voyager 1 Reaches an Extraordinary Deep Space Milestone

While November offers plenty to observe in Earth's skies, something equally remarkable is happening far beyond the planets.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is reaching a historic distance of one light-day from Earth, becoming the first human-made object ever to travel that far from our planet.

A light-day is the distance light travels through space in 24 hours. Because radio signals move at the speed of light, a message transmitted from Earth will require an entire day to reach Voyager 1 at that distance.

If the spacecraft sends a response immediately, the return signal will take another 24 hours to arrive. That means even the fastest possible round-trip communication will require approximately 48 hours.

The milestone illustrates just how far Voyager 1 has traveled since leaving Earth and how challenging it has become to communicate with a spacecraft exploring such distant regions of space.

To get a sense of the spacecraft's current direction, look toward the constellation Ophiuchus, also known as the Serpent Bearer. Voyager 1 is traveling through space in that general direction, far beyond anything visible to the unaided eye.

NASA is marking the achievement on November 17 with its Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day activation, inviting people to celebrate this extraordinary accomplishment in space exploration.

November's Supermoon Begins a Three-Month Celestial Show

The final major skywatching highlight arrives on November 24, when a full supermoon will rise into the evening sky.

A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with a period when the Moon is relatively close to Earth in its orbit. Because the Moon follows a slightly elliptical path rather than a perfect circle, its distance from our planet changes throughout the month.

When a full Moon occurs near the closer portion of that orbit, it can appear somewhat larger and brighter than an average full Moon. Although the difference is real, it is often subtle enough that casual observers may not immediately notice it.

November's event is particularly noteworthy because it begins a sequence of three consecutive supermoons. Another will follow in December, with a third arriving in January.

For an especially memorable view, NASA recommends looking toward the eastern horizon around sunset on November 24, when the full Moon will be rising.

The Moon may seem unusually enormous when it first appears near the horizon. However, much of that dramatic impression comes from a familiar visual phenomenon called the Moon illusion.

This optical effect makes the Moon appear larger when it is close to the horizon than when it is high overhead, even though its actual apparent size changes very little. The illusion can occur during any full Moon, not just a supermoon.

With three meteor showers, a close planetary pairing, a historic Voyager 1 milestone, and the beginning of a supermoon series, November offers plenty of reasons to look up and explore the night sky.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights multiple inspiring celestial events visible to the general public and a historic milestone by NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft becoming the first human-made object to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. These events have broad significance for public engagement with space and science, and the article provides detailed context about each event, making it a substantive and uplifting story about space exploration and natural phenomena.
articles.personality_title: November's Night Sky Offers Meteor Showers, Planet Sights, and Voyager 1 Milestone
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – November 2026 brings many interesting events in the night sky. People can see meteor showers, planets close together, a bright supermoon, and NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft reaching a new distance record.

**What happened** – In early November, two meteor showers called the Southern and Northern Taurids light up the sky, sometimes with bright fireballs. Mid-month, Mars and Jupiter appear very close in the sky, easy to spot without a telescope. On November 17, Voyager 1 becomes the first spacecraft to be one light-day away from Earth, meaning signals take a full day to reach it. Later, the Leonid meteor shower offers more shooting stars, and on November 24 a full supermoon begins a series of three bright moons in a row.

**Impact** – These events give everyone a chance to enjoy space from Earth. The meteor showers and planet pairing are visible to the naked eye, making space feel closer and more exciting. articles.personality_title_es: El cielo de noviembre ofrece lluvias de meteoros, planetas juntos y un hito de Voyager 1
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Noviembre de 2026 trae muchos eventos interesantes en el cielo nocturno. La gente puede ver lluvias de meteoros, planetas cercanos, una superluna brillante y la nave Voyager 1 de la NASA alcanzando un nuevo récord de distancia.

**Qué pasó** – A principios de noviembre, dos lluvias de meteoros llamadas Tauro del Sur y Tauro del Norte iluminan el cielo, a veces con bolas de fuego brillantes. A mediados de mes, Marte y Júpiter se ven muy cerca en el cielo, visibles sin telescopio. El 17 de noviembre, Voyager 1 se convierte en la primera nave en estar a un día luz de la Tierra, lo que significa que las señales tardan un día entero en llegar. Más tarde, la lluvia de meteoros Leónidas ofrece más estrellas fugaces, y el 24 de noviembre una superluna llena comienza una serie de tres lunas brillantes seguidas.

**Impacto** – Estos eventos dan a todos la oportunidad de disfrutar del espacio desde la Tierra. Las lluvias de meteoros y el acercamiento planetario se pueden ver a simple vista, haciendo que el espacio se sienta más cercano y emocionante. El hito de Voyager 1 muestra hasta dónde ha llegado la exploración humana. La luz tarda 24 horas en llegar a la nave, mostrando lo grande que es el espacio y lo difícil que es comunicarse a tanta distancia.

**Próximo paso** – Las personas pueden observar el cielo durante noviembre para ver estos eventos. La celebración de la NASA por la distancia de Voyager 1 invita a aprender sobre la exploración espacial. La serie de superlunas continúa hasta enero, y los movimientos de Marte y Júpiter se pueden seguir en los próximos días. Estos eventos pueden inspirar más interés en la astronomía y la ciencia espacial.

**Resumen en una frase** – Noviembre de 2026 ofrece lluvias de meteoros espectaculares, vistas cercanas de planetas, una superluna brillante y un hito histórico de Voyager 1, invitando a todos a explorar el cielo nocturno.
